To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
acute inflammation affects attentional alerting, but does not affect orienting and executive attention.

inflammation affects the neural network for alerting, but not orienting or executive control, and that the effects of inflammation on alerting are evident at the neural, but not the behavioral, level.
Acute low-grade inflammation is associated with a selective modulation of oscillatory brain activity during attentional alerting, as measured by EEG.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how inflammation influences the brain and behavior.
the impact of low-grade inflammation on cognitive functioning, and in particular, on the ability to allocate and sustain attention.
how inflammation may affect the human attentional network and how such effects may contribute to the experience of illness-related sluggish cognitive tempo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the present findings reveal a selective effect of acute low-grade inflammatory response on the alerting aspect in attention, which may be a key mechanism underlying the perceived cognitive sluggishness associated with inflammation.
the present study demonstrates that the alerting network of the attention system is sensitive to the presence of inflammation.
the present study provides the first evidence of selective effects of inflammation on human attention.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
acute inflammation affects the brain in a selective way that is not necessarily detrimental to performance, and that this effect is most pronounced in the alerting network of attention.
inflammation is associated with greater attentional effort, which may be a contributing factor to cognitive sluggishness.
inflammation can cause a selective effect on attentional processes, and that this effect is reflected in oscillatory activity in the alpha and theta bands.
The main takeaway from our work is that
inflammation is a selective modulator of human attention, which has implications for understanding how inflammation may contribute to cognitive deficits observed during illness and chronic disease.
acute inflammation has a specific impact on attentional alerting and that the effects of this inflammation on the brain are not necessarily reflected in behavioral performance.
acute mild inflammation may have selective and potentially detrimental effects on human attention, and that these effects are not limited to performance decrements, but also manifest in the brain.
